papers.title: Self-selection bias in evaluating the effectiveness of mammography screening: A sensitivity analysis on data from the German screening program
papers.authors: Maria Veronica Vinattieri, Laura Buschmann, Jürgen Wellmann, André Karch, Heike Minnerup, Keith Humphreys
papers.abstract: Self-selection bias in observational studies assessing the effectiveness of a breast cancer screening program can arise when non-participants of screening have worse general health conditions or lower compliance with treatments than screening participants. Building on recently described methodology for tumour progression modelling and causal survival analysis of screening data, our main contribution is to describe approaches to conduct sensitivity analyses for self-selection effects when studying screening effects on all-cause survival and breast cancer cumulative incidence, among screen-detected cases, in a population where all individuals are offered screening. Sensitivity analyses are inspired by an approach to correcting for self-selection bias that has been used for observational studies of mortality. We report simulation studies that demonstrate the impact that a correction factor has on all-cause survival and on the cumulative incidence of breast cancer death following diagnosis. We also apply our methods to estimate the benefit of early detection in non-overdiagnosed screen-detected cancers using data from the German mammography screening program. For sensitivity parameter values, we leverage on data on other (non-breast cancer) cause survival among participants and non-participants of mammography screening in the same study and estimate how counterfactual all-cause survival is improved, and breast cancer cumulative incidence is reduced for patients with screen-detected cancers, when accounting for self-selection bias.

papers.title: Scale-Transformed Power Priors for External Data Integration in Longitudinal Studies
papers.authors: Md Tuhin Sheikh
papers.abstract: Incorporating external data can improve precision in longitudinal studies, but effective borrowing requires that information from different studies be comparable. Within a Bayesian framework, power priors are widely used for external data integration through likelihood discounting. However, they assume that parameters are on a common information scale. In longitudinal settings, differences in follow-up duration, measurement variability, and correlation structure, along with random effects, can lead to differences in effective Fisher information across studies. This complicates parameter comparability and poses challenges for existing methods, which can result in biased or inefficient inference. We propose a scale-transformed power prior for external data integration in longitudinal studies. The method is developed within a linear mixed-effects modeling framework and rescales historical parameters to the current study scale using Fisher information before borrowing. Conditional Fisher information accounts for unobserved random effects and adjusts for study-specific variability. To address differences in variability and correlation structure, we implement a partial borrowing strategy that applies borrowing to fixed effects while allowing variance components to remain study-specific. We introduce a generalized formulation with an additive adjustment component to allow for remaining differences after scaling. Theoretical results characterize how differences in information scale lead to bias under conventional power priors and establish conditions under which the proposed method improves bias and precision. Simulation studies demonstrate improved performance and provide guidance on settings where scale transformation is beneficial. An application to prostate cancer clinical trial data demonstrates the importance of the proposed method.

papers.title: Scalable finite mixture of regression models for clustering species responses in ecology
papers.authors: Francis K C Hui, Patricia Menéndez, Scott Foster, Skip Woolley
papers.abstract: When modeling species assemblages in ecology, clustering species with similar environmental responses can facilitate a more parsimonious understanding of species compositions and improve the prediction of the overall community. One statistical method that implements this idea is species archetype models (SAMs), a type of finite mixture of regression model where species are grouped according to the shape of their environmental response. However, a current shortcoming of SAMs is their computational complexity, hindering their usefulness in cases involving hundreds or thousands of sites and/or species. In this paper, we propose approximate and scalable SAMs (asSAMs) to overcome this drawback. The key to asSAMs lies in constructing a quadratic approximation to individual species-archetype contributions to the marginal likelihood. This results in an objective function resembling a finite mixture of multivariate normal densities, which can be maximized via fully closed-form iterative updates. We demonstrate how asSAMs also promote fast uncertainty quantification using bootstrapping, and variable selection through an additional regularization penalty. Simulation studies and an application to presence-absence records of over 230 species from the Great Barrier Reef Seabed biodiversity project demonstrate that asSAMs can achieve strong estimation, selection, and predictive performance, while being computationally much faster than current methods for fitting SAMs. This makes asSAMs a practical approach for clustering species' environmental responses in high-dimensional species assemblage datasets.

papers.title: Scalable Estimation of Crossed Random Effects Models via Multi-way Discretization
papers.authors: Shota Takeishi, Shonosuke Sugasawa
papers.abstract: Cross-classified data frequently arise in scientific fields such as education, healthcare, and social sciences. A common modeling strategy is to introduce crossed random effects within a regression framework. However, this approach often encounters serious computational bottlenecks, particularly for non-Gaussian outcomes. In this paper, we propose a scalable and flexible method that approximates the distribution of each random effect by a discrete distribution, effectively partitioning the random effects into a finite number of representative values. This approximation allows us to express the model as a multi-way discrete structure, which can be efficiently estimated using a simple and fast iterative algorithm. The proposed method accommodates a wide range of outcome models and remains applicable even in settings with more than two-way cross-classification. We theoretically establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator under general settings of classification levels. Through simulation studies and real data applications, we demonstrate the practical performance of the proposed method in logistic, Poisson, and ordered probit regression models involving cross-classified structures.

papers.title: Sample size determination for randomized decentralized clinical trials with longitudinal outcomes
papers.authors: Chunyi Zhang, Ying Yuan, Ruitao Lin, Suyu Liu
papers.abstract: Decentralized clinical trials (DCTs) offer significant advantages in enhancing trial accessibility, reducing patient burden, and improving population representativeness. These benefits are particularly pronounced in longitudinal trials, where patient outcomes are measured repeatedly over time. However, existing literature lacks appropriate sample size formulas tailored to longitudinal DCTs, which must account for heterogeneous measurement sources and increased uncertainty introduced by decentralized data collection. We propose a unified sample size calculation method for randomized longitudinal DCTs under the generalized linear model framework. The proposed formula is available in closed form and flexibly accommodates a variety of data collection designs, including the simple hybrid design, where all patients contribute both onsite and offsite data, and the stratified hybrid design, where different patient groups may undergo distinct data collection protocols. We also develop estimation procedures to estimate the unknown parameters and compute the sample statistics. Our method further generalizes to accommodate heterogeneous intraclass correlation coefficients, unequal variances between treatment arms, and varying numbers of data collection types or strata. Extensive simulation studies show that the proposed sample size formula achieves robust control of the type I error rate and maintains the desired power across a wide range of realistic scenarios.

papers.title: Sample Size and Power Calculation for Continuous Outcomes in Open-Cohort Stepped Wedge Designs With Multiple Interventions
papers.authors: Shiyu Feng, Meng Zheng, Yi Zhang, Xuezhi Liang, Minglu Yuan, Wen Chen
papers.abstract: Stepped wedge designs with multiple interventions (M-SWDs) are increasingly used to evaluate complex implementation strategies. In many such trials, participants enter and leave over time, giving rise to open-cohort sampling and complex correlation structures. Existing sample size and power calculation methods are largely restricted to single-intervention designs, closed cohorts, or simplified correlation assumptions. We develop a unified, parameter-based framework for sample size and power calculation in open-cohort M-SWDs. The proposed methodology accommodates several common multi-intervention designs, including concurrent, cross-over, supplementation, and factorial designs. Flexible open-cohort sampling schemes are incorporated to account for participant turnover, and both block-exchangeable and decay correlation structures are considered to capture within-cluster and within-individual dependence over time. Closed-form and generalized variance expressions for intervention effect estimators are derived, enabling efficient power calculation under a wide range of design settings. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed formulas provide accurate power estimates, while further power analyses illustrate how the key correlation parameters and participant retention jointly influence power. This work provides practical and theoretically grounded guidance for planning multi-intervention stepped wedge trials under open-cohort sampling, facilitating more realistic and transparent design-stage decision-making.

papers.title: Robustness intervals for competing risks analysis with causes of failure missing not at random
papers.authors: Giorgos Bakoyannis, Aristofanis Rontogiannis, Ying Zhang, Wanzhu Tu, Ann Mwangi, Constantin T Yiannoutsos
papers.abstract: Analysis of competing risks data is often complicated by incomplete or selectively missing information on the cause of failure. Standard approaches typically assume that the cause of failure is missing at random (MAR), an assumption that is generally untestable and frequently implausible in observational studies. We propose a novel sensitivity analysis framework for the proportional cause-specific hazards model that accommodates missing-not-at-random (MNAR) scenarios. A sensitivity parameter is used to quantify the association between missingness and the unobserved cause of failure. Regression coefficients are estimated as functions of this parameter, and a simultaneous confidence band is constructed via a wild bootstrap procedure. This allows identification of a range of MNAR scenarios for which effects remain statistically significant; we refer to this range as a robustness interval. The validity of the proposed approach is justified both theoretically, via empirical process theory, and empirically, through simulation studies. We apply the method to the analysis of data from an HIV cohort study in sub-Saharan Africa, where a substantial proportion of causes of failure are missing and the MAR assumption is implausible. The analysis shows that key findings regarding risk factors for care interruption and mortality are robust across a broad spectrum of MNAR scenarios, underscoring the method's utility in situations with MNAR causes of failure.

papers.title: Robust transfer learning for accelerated failure time model
papers.authors: Chaoqi Wang, Jie Ding, Xiaoguang Wang
papers.abstract: Limited sample sizes can impair the statistical accuracy of traditional survival models, resulting in potentially unsatisfactory conclusions. To address this issue, we propose a robust transfer learning framework for the accelerated failure time model (RTrans-AFT) that enables efficient and flexible information borrowing from an external source. The method accommodates both individual-level and summary-level source data and models differences in regression coefficients between cohorts without requiring identical covariate distributions. To control the degree of transfer, we impose an adaptive lasso penalty to control the discrepancy between the source and target parameters. This allows the method to selectively borrow information from the source cohort in the presence of heterogeneity, while fully incorporating external information when the two cohorts are comparable. Importantly, the framework is robust to potential data irregularities, such as outliers, which are common in real-world survival datasets. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator. Simulation studies demonstrate that RTrans-AFT substantially improves estimation accuracy and achieves notable variance reduction, leading to enhanced statistical efficiency. The practical utility of the method is further illustrated through an analysis of lung adenocarcinoma data, where the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) registry data serve as the external source.

papers.title: Regression Adjusted Target Effects Using Auxiliary Strata Under Design-Based Inference
papers.authors: Zixuan Zhao, Yuehan Yang
papers.abstract: We propose a design-based covariate adjustment that leverages information from auxiliary strata to improve the efficiency of average treatment effect estimation when target samples are sparse. The estimator borrows strength from related strata that may be correlated with the target, yielding gains for studies with limited observations or rare subpopulations. We present the estimator, develop a Neyman-style conservative variance estimator for hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction, and establish its large-sample properties. The procedure is straightforward to implement within standard randomization-based workflows and does not require a correctly specified outcome model or stochastic error assumptions. In simulations, the method delivers lower variance and narrower confidence intervals than conventional design-based or regression-adjusted estimators across a range of sparsity and correlation patterns. Applications to a schooling experiment and the ACTG 175 randomized trial illustrate practical gains in precision.

papers.title: Parsimonious modeling of category-specific effects in partial proportional odds models based on trees
papers.authors: Nikolai Spuck, Ingo Gräff, Moritz Berger
papers.abstract: The proportional odds model is arguably the most widely applied regression approach for ordinal response variables. It assumes that the effects of the covariates are constant across the response categories allowing a parsimonious model specification. A violation of this assumption, however, may lead to biased effect estimates and decreased predictive ability. To overcome this issue, partial proportional odds models, where proportionality is only enforced for a smaller subset of covariates, can be applied. While statistical tests to check the proportional odds assumption are available, a generalized framework for data-driven selection of category-specific effects has not been established. In this paper, we introduce a novel tree-structured algorithm that forms clusters of categories sharing the same effect on the ordinal response, with a focus on model parsimony and ease of interpretation. The proposed model appeared to be superior to alternatives in a clinical application to data from the University Hospital Bonn on patients presenting in the emergency department. The predictive ability and selection properties of the proposed approach were also compared to alternative approaches, such as LASSO-penalized regression, in a simulation study.

papers.title: P4MC: A Monte Carlo Classification Method Based on Partial Variables for Postoperative Complication Prediction
papers.authors: Lingyi Hu, Yao Cui, Qi Yang, Shan Tang, Shanjun Mao
papers.abstract: Predicting postoperative complications is a critical task for improving patient care and optimizing resource management. We formulate the task as a binary classification problem based on two-stage clinical data: preoperative and intraoperative variables. A key difficulty is that intraoperative data are systematically missing for preoperative prediction. Existing methods, which typically rely solely on preoperative data or single intraoperative indicator imputation, generally fail to capture important latent intraoperative information. To provide a more robust solution, we propose P4MC (Preoperative, Partial intraoPerative, and Postoperative Monte Carlo classification). This approach explicitly models the dependence between the two stages to recover latent intraoperative information. Specifically, P4MC first applies partial sufficient dimension reduction (PSDR) to compress intraoperative variables into a low-dimensional sufficient reduction. We then estimate the conditional distribution of this reduction given preoperative variables using nonparametric density estimation and generate latent intraoperative features for classification via Monte Carlo sampling. A simulation study demonstrates the improved predictive performance and stability of P4MC when combined with standard machine learning methods. Applications to two clinical cohorts, laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy and hepatocellular carcinoma, further show that P4MC outperforms conventional approaches and yields clinically interpretable insights. An open-source R program is provided in the P4MC package, available at https://github.com/501fox/P4MC.git.

papers.title: Optimal e-values for testing the mean of a bounded random variable against a composite alternative
papers.authors: S Arnold, E Clerico
papers.abstract: We derive explicitly the e-values with optimal (relative) growth rate in the worst case for testing the mean of a bounded random variable, thereby providing the first application of the (RE)GROW quality criteria beyond the assumption of mutually absolutely continuous hypotheses for e-values originally proposed by Grünwald et al. (2024). For both criteria, we explicitly characterise the alternatives that are most difficult to test against and show that they admit a meaningful interpretation. We give two important examples in which REGROW provides a powerful quality criterion to choose optimal e-variables whereas GROW leads to trivial solutions.

papers.title: Nonparametric modelling of continuous-time Markov chains with scalable exact and approximate gradients
papers.authors: Filippo Monti, Xiang Ji, Yucai Shao, Marc A Suchard
papers.abstract: Inferring the infinitesimal rates of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) is a central challenge in many scientific domains. This task is hindered by 3 factors: quadratic growth in the number of rates as the CTMC state space expands, strong dependencies among rates, and incomplete information for many transitions. We introduce a new Bayesian framework that flexibly models CTMC rates by incorporating covariates through Gaussian processes. This approach improves inference by integrating new information and deepens our understanding of CTMC stochastic behaviour by shedding light on potential external drivers. Unlike previous approaches limited to linear covariate effects, our method captures complex nonlinear relationships, enabling fuller use of covariate information and more accurate characterization of their influence. For efficient posterior inference, we employ Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. To avoid the prohibitive cost of repeated matrix-exponential derivatives under existing approaches, we develop 2 scalable strategies for exact and approximate gradient computation. Given N observations and K CTMC states, these strategies reduce the cost from O(NK3), with a substantial constant, to O(K3+NK2), with cheaper constants. We demonstrate the method in Bayesian phylogenetic and phylogeographic inference, showing strong performance on synthetic and real datasets and empirical quadratic scaling in K, even when N<K.

papers.title: Linear projection inference for Individual Variable Importance
papers.authors: Xinjie Zhou, Zhengbang Li
papers.abstract: Quantifying how the predictive value of biomarkers varies across patient characteristics is central to precision medicine. While Individual Variable Importance (IVI) offers a rigorous framework for this task, existing non-parametric estimators often prove unstable and inefficient in clinical studies with limited sample sizes ($N\lt 500$). To address this, we propose a Linear Projection IVI framework that prioritizes inferential stability over functional flexibility. We formulate the estimator as a first-order approximation to high-dimensional importance surfaces using linear interaction structures. Theoretical results establish that, even under model misspecification, the estimator converges to a well-defined pseudo-true parameter corresponding to the best linear projection of the underlying IVI function. We derive closed-form expressions for local and global importance, prove $\sqrt{N}$-consistency, and introduce a principled "Gatekeeper" hypothesis test. This procedure utilizes a robust joint Wald statistic to control Type I error for heterogeneity detection prior to subgroup stratification, effectively preventing spurious discovery. Simulation studies demonstrate superior finite-sample efficiency relative to kernel-based alternatives and robustness to binary outcome misspecification. Applications to NHANES and Pima Indian diabetes datasets illustrate the framework's utility in distinguishing reproducible biological signals from noise in data-constrained settings.

papers.title: Improving interpretation of latent class models for diagnostic tests: distinguishing target condition from measurands using directed acyclic graphs
papers.authors: Nandini Dendukuri, Ian Schiller, Else Margreet Bijker, Michael Libman, Paul Gustafson, Patrick M Bossuyt, Joanna Merckx
papers.abstract: In the absence of a perfect diagnostic test for a target condition, one or more imperfect tests may be used to arrive at a clinical diagnosis. Latent class analysis can be used to model data from imperfect tests with the objective of estimating test accuracy and target condition prevalence. Such models typically assume there are 2 latent classes underlying the observed data—target condition positive and target condition negative. However, as we illustrate, this would be an oversimplification when any of the observed tests has a measurand that is different from the target condition. We show how a directed acyclic graph can be used to illustrate the relationships between the relevant variables—the observed imperfect test results, their latent measurands, the latent target condition, covariates affecting observed or latent variables, and sources of conditional dependence. We then show how to determine the underlying latent classes and their labels. Finally, we examine how consideration of the measurand of each test impacts the likelihood and identifiability of the latent class model. Using simulation studies, we show how ignoring measurands, which are distinct from the target condition, can lead to mislabeling of the latent classes. We illustrate the value of the proposed approach by re-analyzing 2 datasets used in previously published latent class analyses of tests for pediatric tuberculosis and leptospirosis.

papers.title: Improving gene-based analysis of rare variants through Bayesian variable selection
papers.authors: Jingxiong Xu, Nanwei Wang, Yonathan Brhane, Christopher I Amos, Laurent Briollais
papers.abstract: A common approach for detecting rare variants (RVs) associated with complex human diseases is to perform a gene-based analysis or a region-based test of association. Typically, in a gene-based analysis, all the RVs pertaining to the gene considered are included in the statistical test, which potentially reduces its power since most RVs are likely not associated with the outcome of interest. As paradigm shift, we propose to add a variable selection step to choose the RVs that compose the gene-based test statistic as a way to enhance the power of the test. We propose a Bayes factor (BF) test statistic derived from the generalized linear model and its conjugate prior. A key component of our approach is the selection of the important RVs within a gene, which is performed through a birth-death Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm. Our approach can also leverage functional annotation at the RV level through the elicitation of the conjugate prior. Through simulation studies, we show that the proposed BF outperformed competing approaches both in terms of gene ranking and power to detect gene-based associations. The power of BF was improved by the use of the variable selection procedure and this gain of power was more substantial when functional annotation was included in this procedure. The application of our new approach to a large whole-exome sequencing data set comparing 1658 individuals with lung cancer to 1492 healthy controls was able to identify new genes associated with lung cancer and pointed towards interesting cancer-related pathways.

papers.title: Factor-Augmented Neural Conditional Density Estimation with Application to Drug Response Prediction
papers.authors: Weineng Zhu, Xiaoyu Sheng
papers.abstract: High-dimensional pharmacogenomic data pair thousands of molecular features with hundreds of cancer cell lines, complicating conditional density estimation. We study factor-augmented CINDES, which estimates conditional response densities from principal-component scores through binary classification. For an honest pilot/main-sample construction, assuming fresh-score PCA recovery, we derive a risk bound separating conditional-density learning, PCA score error, and representation bias. This guarantee does not cover the implemented procedure, which reuses observations for PCA and CINDES. In favorable strong-factor simulations, PCA improved a fixed CINDES pipeline, but PCA-MDN achieved lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) and integrated L 1 error in the matched comparison. Stress tests showed losses from omitted response-relevant low-variance directions and weak factor recovery, with sample-size-dependent factor-count effects. Across all 692 eligible source-specific genomics of drug sensitivity in cancer (GDSC) units and five splits, mean held-out NLL was 1.5414 for PCA-CINDES, versus 1.5661 and 1.5557 for ElasticNet and PCA/Ridge Gaussian models; PCA-MDN was better at 1.5156. A previously fixed 35-unit audit favored PCA-CINDES over Raw-X CINDES (mean paired NLL difference - 0 . 178 ) and found lower measured computational cost. The evidence supports PCA compression when retained factors capture response information and are accurately estimated; it does not establish robustness to general nonlinear or nonfactor structures, or CINDES as the preferred second-stage estimator. The application concerns preclinical prediction rather than clinical utility.

papers.title: Dynamic borrowing via covariate-adjusted self-adapting mixture priors in clinical trials
papers.authors: Yeonhee Park
papers.abstract: Incorporating historical data into clinical trials can enhance statistical power, but it risks introducing bias if historical and current populations differ. Existing Bayesian borrowing methods often apply a single, prespecified weight to historical data, failing to account for patient-level covariate differences. To address this, we propose a covariate-adjusted self-adapting mixture (CASAM) prior, a Bayesian framework that enables covariate-dependent dynamic borrowing from external data. CASAM adaptively determines the degree of information borrowing by assessing the compatibility between historical and current data conditional on covariates, automatically down-weighting historical information when residual heterogeneity is detected. To further address covariate distribution mismatch between historical and current trials, we develop a propensity-score-integrated implementation of CASAM, which first re-weights historical controls to align their covariate distribution with that of the current control arm before applying the CASAM prior. This layered strategy allows CASAM to focus on structural similarity while the propensity-score adjustment corrects for population-level imbalance. Together, CASAM and its propensity-score-based implementation provide an empirical-Bayes framework for adaptive borrowing that combines covariate alignment with outcome-model compatibility assessment.

papers.title: Dissecting microbial community structure and heterogeneity via multivariate covariate-adjusted clustering
papers.authors: Zhongmao Liu, Xiaohui Yin, Yanjiao Zhou, Gen Li, Kun Chen
papers.abstract: In microbiome studies, it is often of great interest to identify clusters or partitions of microbiome profiles within a study population and to characterize the distinctive attributes of each resulting microbial community. While raw counts or relative compositions are commonly used for such analysis, variations between clusters may be driven or distorted by subject-level covariates, reflecting underlying biological and clinical heterogeneity across individuals. Simultaneously detecting latent communities and identifying covariates that differentiate them can enhance our understanding of the microbiome and its association with health outcomes. To this end, we propose a Dirichlet-multinomial mixture regression (DMMR) model that enables joint clustering of microbiome profiles while accounting for covariates with either homogeneous or heterogeneous effects across clusters. A novel symmetric link function is introduced to facilitate covariate modeling through the compositional parameters. We develop efficient algorithms with convergence guarantees for parameter estimation and establish theoretical properties of the proposed estimators. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in clustering, feature selection, and heterogeneity detection. We illustrate the utility of DMMR through a comprehensive application to upper-airway microbiota data from a pediatric asthma study, uncovering distinct microbial subtypes and their associations with clinical characteristics.

papers.title: Dimension reduction for characterizing sexual dimorphism in biomechanics of the temporomandibular joint
papers.authors: Sung Hee Park, Xin Zhang, Elizabeth H Slate, Shuchun Sun, Hai Yao
papers.abstract: Sexual dimorphism is a critical factor in many biological and medical research fields. In biomechanics and bioengineering, understanding sex differences is crucial for studying musculoskeletal conditions such as temporomandibular disorder. This paper focuses on the association between the craniofacial skeletal morphology and temporomandibular joint related masticatory muscle attachments to discern sex differences. Data were collected from 11 female and 10 male cadaver heads to investigate sex-specific relationships between the skull and muscles. We propose a conditional cross-covariance reduction (CCR) model, designed to examine the dynamic association between two sets of random variables conditioned on a third binary variable (e.g., sex), highlighting the most distinctive sex-related relationships between skull and muscle attachments in the human cadaver data. Under the CCR model, we employ a sparse singular value decomposition algorithm. We further introduce a sequential permutation for selecting sparsity method to identify important variables and determine the optimal number of selected variables.

papers.title: Causal inference with dyadic data in randomized experiments
papers.authors: Yilin Li, Lu Deng, Yong Wang, Wang Miao
papers.abstract: Estimating treatment effects in networked settings is a central challenge in online controlled experiments, particularly on social media platforms. We investigate a scenario where the unit-level outcome of interest comprises a series of dyadic outcomes that record pairwise interactions between units, ranging from point-to-point messaging at the microscale to bilateral trade flows at the macroscale. Because the response is defined at the dyadic level, the treatment assigned to one unit can affect the outcomes of all dyads that involve it, inducing a form of network interference. We propose a design-based causal inference framework for randomized experiments with dyadic outcomes. Within this framework, we propose estimators of the global average treatment effect under Bernoulli, complete, and cluster randomization, derive the convergence rates, and establish a central limit theorem for Bernoulli randomization. We further construct a class of variance estimators that are asymptotically conservative and establish asymptotic confidence-interval guarantees under degree and variance-scale conditions. Numerical studies show that the proposed estimators can reduce bias and mean squared error relative to estimators based on unit-level outcomes in a range of finite-sample settings. We illustrate the methods using two large-scale online experiments, evaluating the impact of a recommendation algorithm and a calling feature.

papers.title: Bivariate Copula Models With Event-Free Cure Effect for Survival Extrapolations and Individual-Level Correlation Analysis
papers.authors: Daniel J Sharpe, Georgia Yates, Tuli De, Renuka Kandikatla, Prianka Singh, Matthew Dixon, Kiran Davé, Jackie Vanderpuye-Orgle, Murat Kurt
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Overall survival (OS) extrapolations from mixture cure models (MCMs) are often sensitive to the cure fraction, which is challenging to estimate when data are immature. Furthermore, in some cancer populations, it may be unreasonable to assume curative effects among patients who are not event-free. We addressed these problems using bivariate copula MCMs to jointly model OS and progression- (PFS) or recurrence-free survival (RFS), with a single event-free cure fraction parameter. METHODS: We proposed a practical framework for parametric survival copula model selection and interpretation, which involves estimating five representative candidate copula functions and examining OS distributions conditioned on intermediate event times. Bivariate MCMs with event-free cure fraction, based on previously selected marginal distributions, were estimated for two studies of nivolumab with contrasting survival patterns, namely, in previously treated advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (OS-PFS correlation) and resected melanoma (OS-RFS correlation). RESULTS: OS extrapolations from bivariate MCMs with an effective PFS (or RFS) cure fraction were more conservative than from univariate MCMs. Although patient-level OS-PFS/RFS correlation coefficients were sensitive to the copula, model averaging and inspecting estimated conditional OS distributions enabled clinically meaningful inference on the prognostic impact of intermediate events. CONCLUSIONS: Bivariate MCMs with event-free cured subpopulation incorporated curative effects into OS extrapolations more cautiously than conventional MCMs, based on a more rapidly maturing composite endpoint. The model is especially useful when OS data are immature and if post-event cure is clinically implausible. Employing alternative copulas that cover archetypal association patterns mitigated model selection bias in patient-level correlation analysis.

papers.title: Beyond Pre-Trends: The Case for Routine Placebo Falsification in Difference-in-Differences Health Policy Research
papers.authors: S M Hasan Ul Bari, Marshia Rahman
papers.abstract: No new empirical data were generated. The simulation code (Python) that reproduces Table 1, Figure 1, and Supporting Figure S1 is provided as Supporting Information. Figure S1: Rejection rates (α = 0.05) of the joint Wald test of the five leads, the time-shifted placebo (Periods 4–6 vs. 1–3), and the negative control outcome DiD, as the size of each violation increases. (a) Linear differential drift of 0 to 0.30 error standard deviations per period (Scenario B). (b) Shock coinciding with the policy of 0 to 1.5 error standard deviations (Scenario C). The x-axis shows the resulting bias of the main DiD estimate. Same design as Table 1 (50 units, 25 treated, 10 periods, policy from Period 7, AR(1) errors with ρ = 0.5); 2000 replications per point. The negative control outcome receives the shock in (b) but no drift in (a). In (a), bias = 5 × drift per period (drift 0 to 0.30). The dashed line marks the nominal 5% level; in (b) the two pre-period diagnostics overlap at this level (4.3% to 5.4%). Monte Carlo standard error ≤ 0.011. Supplementary S1: Data S1: Python simulation code reproducing Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure S1. Any queries (other than missing content) should be directed to the corresponding author for the article.

papers.title: An efficient Bayesian data augmentation algorithm for continuous-time stochastic epidemic models fit to partially observed incidence data
papers.authors: Haoyu Wu, David A Stephens, Erica E M Moodie
papers.abstract: Statistical modeling of infectious disease outbreaks with incidence data is crucial to understanding epidemic dynamics and informing public health interventions. Stochastic epidemic models (SEMs) account for the inherent stochasticity in epidemic evolution and are particularly useful in small outbreaks or low-prevalence settings. In SEMs, the epidemic is naturally represented as a continuous-time Markov jump process (MJP), while surveillance data are collected at discrete times and subject to underdetection. Fitting SEMs to partially observed epidemic trajectories requires integrating over all possible transition paths, which is often intractable. Individual-level data augmentation (DA) methods have been developed to address these challenges. However, existing approaches either rely on per-subject updates with limited scalability or impose typically unrealistic assumptions to simplify the complex dimensional change problem for state-space SEMs. We present an efficient DA Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework for fitting continuous-time state-space SEMs to incidence data. Our method uses a block sampler to jointly update individual trajectories and proposes transition times using a discrete-time approximation to the latent MJP. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that our method significantly improves MCMC mixing and scalability compared to the previous DA approach and remains computationally robust in scenarios where particle MCMC algorithms struggle. We apply the method to the 2014 Ebola outbreak in a rural village in Sierra Leone and the 2009 H1N1 outbreak in a remote community in Canada.

papers.title: ACS: An interactive framework for conformal selection
papers.authors: Yu Gui, Ying Jin, Yash Nair, Zhimei Ren
papers.abstract: This paper presents adaptive conformal selection (ACS), an interactive framework for model-free selection with guaranteed error control. Building on conformal selection (Jin and Candès, 2023b), ACS generalizes the approach to support human-in-the-loop adaptive data analysis. Under the ACS framework, we can partially reuse the data to boost the selection power, make decisions on the fly while exploring the data, and incorporate new information or preferences as they arise. The key to ACS is a carefully designed principle that controls the information available for decision making, allowing the data analyst to explore the data adaptively while maintaining rigorous control of the false discovery rate (FDR). Based on the ACS framework, we provide concrete selection algorithms for various goals, including model update/selection, diversified selection, and incorporating newly available labeled data. The effectiveness of ACS is demonstrated through extensive numerical simulations and real-data applications in large language model (LLM) deployment and drug discovery.

papers.title: Using fractional derivatives to derive marginal densities
papers.authors: S Y Li, D A van Dyk, M Autenrieth
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel method for analytical derivations of marginal densities using the fractional derivatives of moment-generating functions. Although the method requires likelihood functions to take specific forms, its assumptions are otherwise modest. It only requires that the prior moment-generating functions exist, are finite, and are continuous and differentiable at certain points. We also present the probabilistic and statistical insights behind this method.

papers.title: Two-Stage Estimation for Causal Inference Involving Semi-Continuous Exposures
papers.authors: Xiaoya Wang, Richard J Cook, Yeying Zhu, Tugba Akkaya-Hocagil, R Colin Carter, Sandra W Jacobson, Joseph L Jacobson, Louise M Ryan
papers.abstract: Methods for causal inference are well developed for binary and continuous exposures, but in many settings, the exposure has a substantial mass at zero-such exposures are called semi-continuous. We propose a general causal framework for such semi-continuous exposures, together with a two-stage estimation strategy. A two-part propensity structure is introduced for the semi-continuous exposure, with one component for exposure status (exposed vs unexposed) and another for the exposure level among those exposed, and incorporates both into a marginal structural model that disentangles the effects of exposure status and dose. The two-stage procedure sequentially targets the causal dose-response among exposed individuals and the causal effect of exposure status at a reference dose, allowing flexibility in the choice of propensity score methods in the second stage. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the resulting estimators, and characterize their limiting values under misspecification of the propensity score models. Simulation studies evaluate finite sample performance and robustness, and an application to a study of prenatal alcohol exposure and child cognition demonstrates how the proposed methods can be used to address a range of scientific questions about both exposure status and exposure intensity.

papers.title: Test of partial effects for Fréchet regression on Bures-Wasserstein manifolds
papers.authors: Haoshu Xu, Hongzhe Li
papers.abstract: We propose a novel test for assessing partial effects in Fréchet regression on the Bures-Wasserstein manifold. Under the null hypothesis, we show that the statistic admits a degenerate V-statistic approximation whose limiting distribution is aweighted mixture of chi-squared random variables, with weights determined by the eigenvalues of an integral operator associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) kernel. We establish the asymptotic validity and consistency of the proposed test. Its finite-sample performance is examined through simulation studies.We apply the proposed test to study the effect of age, while controlling for other covariates, on gene co-expression structure in single-cell data.

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis for the Test-Negative Design
papers.authors: Soumyabrata Kundu, Peng Ding, Jingshu Wang, Xinran Li
papers.abstract: The test-negative design has become popular for evaluating the effectiveness of post-licensure vaccines using observational data. In addition to its logistical convenience on data collection, the design is also believed to control for the differential health-care-seeking behavior between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, an important while often unmeasured confounder between the vaccination and infection. Hence, the design has been employed routinely to monitor seasonal flu vaccines and more recently to measure the COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness. Despite its popularity, the design has been questioned, in particular about its ability to fully control for the unmeasured confounding. In this paper, we explore deviations from a perfect test-negative design, and propose various sensitivity analysis methods for estimating the effect of vaccination measured by the causal odds ratio on the subpopulation of individuals with good health-care-seeking behavior. We start with point identification of the causal odds ratio under a test-negative design, comparing different forms of identification assumptions and their corresponding estimands. We then propose two approaches for conducting sensitivity analysis, addressing the influence of the unmeasured confounding in two different ways. Specifically, one approach investigates partial control for unmeasured confounding in the test-negative design, while the other examines the impact of unmeasured confounding on both vaccination and infection. Furthermore, we combine these approaches to provide narrower bounds on the true causal odds ratio, and further sharpen the bounds by restricting the treatment effect heterogeneity. Finally, we apply the proposed methods to evaluate the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines using observational data from test-negative designs.

papers.title: POLAR: A Pessimistic Model-based Policy Learning Algorithm for Dynamic Treatment Regimes
papers.authors: Ruijia Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang, Zhengling Qi, Yue Wu, Yanxun Xu
papers.abstract: Dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) provide a principled framework for optimizing sequential decision-making in domains where decisions must adapt over time in response to individual trajectories, such as healthcare, education, and digital interventions. However, existing statistical methods often rely on strong positivity assumptions and lack robustness under partial data coverage, while offline reinforcement learning approaches typically focus on average training performance, lack statistical guarantees, and require solving complex optimization problems. To address these challenges, we propose POLAR, a novel pessimistic model-based policy learning algorithm for offline DTR optimization. POLAR estimates the transition dynamics from offline data and quantifies uncertainty for each history-action pair. A pessimistic penalty is then incorporated into the reward function to discourage actions with high uncertainty. Unlike many existing methods that focus on average training performance or provide guarantees only for an oracle policy, POLAR directly targets the suboptimality of the final learned policy and offers theoretical guarantees, without relying on computationally intensive minimax or constrained optimization procedures. To the best of our knowledge, POLAR is the first model-based DTR method to provide both statistical and computational guarantees, including finite-sample bounds on policy suboptimality. Empirical results on both synthetic data and the MIMIC-III dataset demonstrate that POLAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods and yields near-optimal, history-aware treatment strategies.

papers.title: Online Updating Mixture Cure Models for Large-Scale Survival Data Streams
papers.authors: Li Jin, Tao Hu, Liming Xiang
papers.abstract: The growing availability of large-scale survival data streams present significant challenges for statistical inference particularly in the presence of a cure fraction, which complicates estimation and increases computational burden. To address these challenges, we propose an online updating mixture cure model framework. Our approach employs a batchwise renewable estimation procedure that aggregates historical information into summary statistics to update the model without retaining historical individual-level data, and thus eliminating the need for full data storage. A renewable penalized expectation-maximization algorithm is developed to enable simultaneous parameter estimation and variable selection. Furthermore, a tuning-free strategy is incorporated to enhance computational efficiency. The asymptotic properties of the proposed method are established. Simulation studies and an application to breast cancer data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results database demonstrate the method's estimation accuracy, predictive performance, and computational scalability.

papers.title: Multivariate Poisson intensity estimation via low-rank tensor decomposition
papers.authors: Haotian Xu, Carlos Misael Madrid Padilla, Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla, Daren Wang
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose new matrix- and tensor-based methodologies for estimating multivariate intensity functions of inhomogeneous point processes. By viewing multivariate intensity functions as infinite-dimensional matrices or tensors within function spaces, our algorithms attain the optimal bias-variance trade-off, yielding rate-optimal estimation error, with model complexity governed by matrix or tensor ranks. They substantially improve estimation accuracy, while simultaneously reducing computational cost. To illustrate the adaptivity of the proposed framework, we show that many fundamental classes of multivariate functions, including additive and mean-field models, admit finite-rank tensor representations. We apply our method to a four-dimensional U.S. Geological Survey earthquake dataset, comprising features such as latitude, longitude, depth, and magnitude. Our tensor estimator recovers localized seismicity patterns (California, Oklahoma, Pacific Northwest, north-central U.S.), whereas the kernel baseline oversmooths them.

papers.title: Localizing support-set changepoints in high-dimensional linear models
papers.authors: Junfeng Cui, Junhui Wang, Changliang Zou, Yan Zhou
papers.abstract: Existing changepoint localization methods for high-dimensional regression models typically focus on scenarios where the regression coefficients follow a piecewise constant structure over time. However, this assumption can be overly restrictive in many practical applications due to the complex temporal dynamics of the coefficients. Additionally, in sparse regression models, the primary interest sometimes lies not in changes in the magnitudes of the coefficients, but rather in identifying the time points at which covariates transition between inactive and active states. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for detecting changepoints in the support set, allowing the coefficients to vary continuously over time. Theoretically, we establish the minimax lower bound on the localization error that nearly matches the upper bound achieved by the proposed method, and show that the required signal-to-noise condition is essentially the weakest possible based on the impossibility region in a minimax sense. Extensive numerical studies further demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method. It is also applied in the analysis of real air quality data from Northern Taiwan in 2015. An R package "SCP" is developed to implement the proposed method.

papers.title: General Frameworks for Conditional Two-Sample Testing
papers.authors: Seongchan Lee, Suman Cha, Ilmun Kim
papers.abstract: We study the problem of conditional two-sample testing, which aims to determine whether two populations have the same distribution after accounting for confounding factors. This problem commonly arises in various applications, such as domain adaptation and algorithmic fairness, where comparing two groups is essential while controlling for confounding variables. We begin by establishing a hardness result for conditional two-sample testing, demonstrating that no valid test can have significant power against any single alternative without proper assumptions. We then introduce two general frameworks that implicitly or explicitly target specific classes of distributions for their validity and power. Our first framework allows us to convert any conditional independence test into a conditional two-sample test in a black-box manner, while preserving the asymptotic properties of the original conditional independence test. The second framework transforms the problem into comparing marginal distributions with estimated density ratios, which enables direct application of existing methods for marginal two-sample testing. We demonstrate this idea in a concrete manner with classification and kernel-based methods. Finally, simulation studies are conducted to illustrate the proposed frameworks in finite-sample scenarios.

papers.title: Enhancing visual interpretability and explainability in functional survival trees and forests
papers.authors: Giuseppe Loffredo, Elvira Romano, Fabrizio Maturo
papers.abstract: Functional survival models are key tools for analyzing time-to-event data with complex predictors, such as functional or high-dimensional inputs. Despite their predictive strength, these models often lack interpretability, which limits their value in practical decision-making and risk analysis. This study investigates two key survival models: the functional survival tree (FST) and the functional random survival forests (FRSFs). It introduces novel methods and tools to enhance the interpretability of FST models and improve the explainability of FRSF ensembles. Applications to simulated data and to a real intensive care dataset illustrate that the proposed approaches provide post-hoc graphical and functional summaries that facilitate the interpretation of FSTs and the explanation of forest-level predictions.

papers.title: Developing an Innovative Jackknife Estimator for Quantifying Between-Study Variance in Meta-Analysis of Proportions
papers.authors: Muhammad Mohsin, Stephan Morgenthaler
papers.abstract: The DerSimonian and Laird (DL) method, commonly used in meta-analysis, often underestimates the between-study variance. The underestimation causes the confidence intervals to have less than the expected 95% coverage, resulting in inconclusive research findings. The present study introduces the use of the jackknife technique to improve the DL between-study variance estimator for meta-analyses of proportions from single-arm studies, as well as suggests certain transformations in combination with the jackknife technique. The proposed methodology is intended for settings in which the parameter of interest is an event probability or proportion, particularly for small numbers of studies with large variation. Simulation studies for binomial observations are conducted to compare the relative biases and coverage probabilities of the mean ( μ ) obtained by the DL, Paule and Mandel (PM), Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML), and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) methods with our proposed DerSimonian and Laird jackknife (DLJ) and transformed DerSimonian and Laird jackknife (TDLJs) methods. The simulation results show that our proposed DLJ and TDLJ estimators better quantify the between-study variance in meta-analysis of binary events, especially for small numbers of studies with larger variation and high probability of μ respectively. Three real life examples are presented to determine the performance of our new proposed between-study variance estimators.

papers.title: Can discrete-time analyses be trusted for stepped wedge trials with continuous recruitment?
papers.authors: Hao Wang, Guangyu Tong, Heather Allore, Kelsey L Grantham, Monica Taljaard, Fan Li
papers.abstract: In stepped wedge cluster randomized trials (SW-CRTs), the intervention is rolled out to clusters sequentially over multiple periods. It is common practice to analyze data from SW-CRTs using linear mixed models that treat time as discrete. However, a recent systematic review found that 95.1% of cross-sectional SW-CRTs recruit individuals continuously over time. Despite the prevalence of continuous recruitment, there has been limited guidance on how to draw model-robust inference for such designs. In this article, we conduct simulation studies to examine the performance of discrete-time linear mixed models in the case of continuous recruitment designs with a continuous outcome. Specifically, we generate outcomes under a continuous-time exponential decay correlation structure with either discrete or continuous fixed period effects. We consider constant and exposure-time-dependent intervention effects, with and without random intervention effects across clusters. We then analyze the simulated data using linear mixed models under three discrete-time working correlation structures: simple exchangeable, nested exchangeable, and discrete-time exponential decay, with robust sandwich variance estimation. Our results demonstrate that discrete-time analysis often yields negligible bias and that the robust variance estimator with the Mancl and DeRouen correction consistently achieves nominal coverage and type I error rate. However, when recruitment patterns vary systematically between control and intervention periods, discrete-time analyses give slightly biased intervention effect estimates. Finally, we illustrate these findings by reanalyzing a completed SW-CRT.

papers.title: Calibrated Bayes Analysis of Cluster-Randomized Trials
papers.authors: Ruyi Liu, Joshua L Warren, Yuki Ohnishi, Donna Spiegelman, Liangyuan Hu, Fan Li
papers.abstract: In cluster-randomized trials (CRTs), entire clusters of individuals are randomized to treatment, and outcomes within a cluster are typically correlated. While frequentist approaches are standard practice for CRT analysis, Bayesian methods have emerged as a strong alternative. Previous work has investigated the use of Bayesian hierarchical models for continuous, binary, and count outcomes in CRTs, but these approaches focus on model-based treatment effect coefficients as the target estimands, which may have ambiguous interpretation under model misspecification and informative cluster size. In this article, we introduce a calibrated Bayesian procedure for estimand-aligned analysis of CRTs even in the presence of potentially misspecified models. We propose estimators targeting both the cluster-average treatment effect (cluster-ATE) and individual-average treatment effect (individual-ATE), particularly in scenarios with informative cluster sizes. We additionally explore strategies for summarizing the posterior samples that can achieve the frequentist coverage even under working model misspecification. We provide simulation evidence to demonstrate the model-robustness property of the proposed estimators in CRTs, and further investigate the impact of covariate adjustment as well as the use of more flexible Bayesian nonparametric working models in the CRT context.

papers.title: Beyond vintage rotation: bias-free sparse representation learning with oracle inference
papers.authors: Chengyu Cui, Yunxiao Chen, Jing Ouyang, Gongjun Xu
papers.abstract: Learning low-dimensional latent representations is a central topic in statistics and machine learning, and rotation methods have long been used to obtain sparse and interpretable representations. Despite nearly a century of widespread use across many fields, rigorous guarantees for valid inference for the learned representation remain lacking. In this paper, we identify a surprisingly prevalent phenomenon that suggests a reason for this gap: for a broad class of vintage rotations, the resulting estimators exhibit a non-estimable bias. Because this bias is independent of the data, it fundamentally precludes the development of valid inferential procedures, including the construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. To address this challenge, we propose a novel bias-free rotation method within a general representation learning framework based on latent variables. We establish an oracle inference property for the learned sparse representations: the estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance as in the ideal setting where the latent variables are observed. To bridge the gap between theory and computation, we develop an efficient computational framework and prove that its output estimators retain the same oracle property. Our results provide a rigorous inference procedure for the rotated estimators, yielding statistically valid and interpretable representation learning.

papers.title: Bayesian multiple imputation for functional data
papers.authors: Ziren Jiang, Lei Xuan, Eric F Lock, Erjia Cui
papers.abstract: Missing data are pervasive in modern functional datasets, where trajectories are often sparsely or irregularly observed. Although functional principal component analysis is widely used to reconstruct incomplete curves, existing approaches typically employ single imputation, leading to overly optimistic inferences in downstream analyses. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Bayesian multiple imputation framework for functional data (BAMIFun). For single-level functional data, we impose a Bayesian low-rank model that incorporates penalized spline representations to enforce smoothness of the functional domain and derive an efficient Gibbs sampler algorithm for posterior computation. In addition, we demonstrate and validate how to properly account for estimation uncertainties in downstream analysis. Furthermore, we extend the framework to multiway functional data using Functional Tensor Singular Value Decomposition model, enabling Bayesian multiple imputation in settings not supported by existing methods. Simulation studies show that BAMIFun achieves substantially improved coverage and more reliable downstream inference compared to existing methods, while maintaining similar imputation accuracy. Case studies using a physical activity dataset and an infant gut microbiome dataset further demonstrate the practical advantages of our proposed methods under severe missingness.

papers.title: Asymptotic theory of the quadratic assignment procedure for dyadic data analysis
papers.authors: Lei Shi, Peng Ding
papers.abstract: The quadratic assignment procedure (QAP) is a popular tool for analysing dyadic data in medical and social sciences. To test the association between 2 dyadic measurements represented by 2 symmetric matrices, QAP calculates the p-value by permuting the units, or equivalently, by permuting the rows and columns of 1 matrix in the same way. Its extension to the regression setting, known as the multiple regression QAP, has also gained popularity, especially in psychometrics. However, the statistical theory for QAP has not been fully established in the literature. We fill the gap in this paper. We formulate the dyadic models underlying various QAPs. We derive (a) the asymptotic sampling distributions of some canonical test statistics and (b) the corresponding asymptotic permutation distributions induced by QAP under strong and weak null hypotheses. Task (a) relies on applying the theory of U-statistics, and task (b) relies on applying the theory of double-indexed permutation statistics. Our asymptotic theory combines tasks (a) and (b), and suggests that we must use properly studentized statistics in QAP to ensure that it is finite-sample exact under the strong null hypothesis and preserves the asymptotic type I error rate under the weak null hypothesis.

papers.title: A Tail Likelihood Ratio Method for Large-scale Causal Mediation Tests in Epigenome-Wide Studies
papers.authors: Haoyu Yang, Ruoyu Wang, Yuzhou Lin, Xihong Lin

papers.title: Which Small-Sample Correction Should be Used When Analyzing Stepped-Wedge Designs With Time-Varying Treatment Effects?
papers.authors: Yongdong Ouyang, Monica Taljaard, James P Hughes, Fan Li
papers.abstract: Stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials (SW-CRTs) evaluate interventions that are sequentially rolled out across clusters. Standard analyses of SW-CRTs typically use immediate-treatment (IT) models, which assume the treatment effects begin at crossover and remain constant thereafter. When treatment effects vary with exposure duration, IT models may misrepresent the target effects. Exposure-time indicator (ETI) models address this by allowing treatment effects to differ by time since exposure and can properly target the time-averaged treatment effect (TATE) and long-term effect (LTE). Like IT models, ETI models require specification of a random-effects structure, which may be misspecified. While robust variance estimators (RVEs) theoretically protect against such misspecification, their empirical performance under ETI models is not well understood. We review RVEs for ETI models and evaluate them in comprehensive simulation studies with continuous and binary outcomes under correctly specified (binary only) and misspecified random-effects structures. We compare the classic sandwich variance, Kauermann-Carroll (KC), Mancl-DeRouen (MD), and Morel-Bokossa-Neerchal (MBN) bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators for inference on the TATE and LTE in primary simulations and additionally evaluate Fay-Graubard (FG) in a sub-study. Our simulations show that under misspecified random-effects structures, model-based standard errors (SE) produced undercoverage, whereas RVEs improved performance under the ETI models. For continuous outcomes, MD with a t-distribution and degrees of freedom equal to the number of clusters minus two gave the closest to nominal coverage probabilities. Surprisingly, however, MBN was the only consistently reliable option for binary outcomes. MD, however, could be unstable in one-cluster-per-sequence designs because of data sparsity. Across scenarios, both model-based SE and RVE for LTE were unstable, indicating that greater caution is needed when targeting LTE under ETI models.

papers.title: Variable Selection for Additive Global Fréchet Regression
papers.authors: Haoyi Yang, Satarupa Bhattacharjee, Lingzhou Xue, Bing Li
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework for variable selection in Fréchet regression with responses in general metric spaces, a setting increasingly relevant for analyzing non-Euclidean data such as probability distributions and covariance matrices. Building on the concept of (weak) Fréchet conditional means, we develop an additive regression model that represents the metric-based discrepancy of the response as a sum of covariate-specific nonlinear functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). To address the absence of linear structure in the response space, we transform the response via squared distances, enabling an interpretable and tractable additive decomposition. Variable selection is performed using Elastic Net regularization, extended to the RKHS setting, and further refined through a local linear approximation scheme that incorporates folded concave penalty functions. We establish theoretical guarantees, including variable selection consistency and the strong oracle property, under minimal assumptions tailored to metric-space-valued responses. Simulations and applications to distributional and matrix-valued data demonstrate the scalability, interpretability, and practical effectiveness of the proposed approach. This work provides a principled foundation for statistical learning with random object data.

papers.title: Treatment comparisons using a measurement during follow-up and a right-censored time-to-event outcome
papers.authors: Michal Kicinski
papers.abstract: In clinical trials, the comparison between treatment arms of a measurement is often complicated by an event such as death or progression that can make this measurement irrelevant or difficult to perform. In this article, an approach is proposed to compare treatment arms using the net treatment benefit or the win ratio. A more favorable outcome (win) for the experimental arm is defined as the event of (1) a longer time to event for a patient in the experimental arm compared to a patient from the control arm until a prespecified restriction time ϵ or (2) a more favorable outcome with respect to the measurement during follow-up for a patient from the experimental arm and the time to event greater than ϵ for both patients. An estimator is proposed. A simulation study showed approximately no bias. The methodology is illustrated using a leukemia trial.

papers.title: Testing matrix factor structure via generalized likelihood ratio
papers.authors: Xinbing Kong, Liwen Zhang, Tong Zhang
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a generalized likelihood ratio test for assessing whether the factor loading matrix in high-dimensional data exhibits a Kronecker structure, thereby offering a rigorous tool for validating two-way matrix factor models. A central challenge in likelihood-based inference for factor models arises from inherent rotational non-identifiability, which prevents the likelihood function from admitting a standard second-order Taylor expansion. To address this issue, we augment the quasi-likelihood with a quadratic identification penalty that removes rotational degeneracy locally. Building on this construction, we derive the asymptotic distribution of the proposed statistic under the null hypothesis and unveil a new Wilks-type phenomenon in a high-dimensional setting. Under the alternative hypothesis, we further establish the consistency of the test, demonstrating its ability to detect deviations from the Kronecker structure. Simulation studies demonstrate the finite-sample effectiveness of the proposed method. Furthermore, applications to real datasets illustrate the practical utility of the proposed procedure by assessing the presence of Kronecker structure in factor loading matrices.

papers.title: Semiparametric learning from open-set label shift data
papers.authors: Siyan Liu, Yukun Liu, Qinglong Tian, Pengfei Li, Jing Qin
papers.abstract: We study the open-set label shift problem, where the test data may include a novel class absent from the training data. This setting is challenging because both the class proportions and the distribution of the novel class are not identifiable without extra assumptions. Existing approaches often rely on restrictive separability conditions, prior knowledge, or computationally infeasible procedures, and some may lack theoretical guarantees. We propose a semiparametric density ratio model framework that ensures identifiability while allowing overlap between novel and known classes. Within this framework, we develop maximum empirical likelihood estimators and confidence intervals for class proportions, establish their asymptotic validity, and design a stable Expectation–Maximization algorithm for computation. We also develop a goodness-of-fit test for model assessment and an approximately optimal classifier with theoretical guarantees. Simulations and a real-data application confirm that our methods improve both estimation accuracy and classification performance compared with existing approaches.

papers.title: Semi-supervised Clustering Through Representation Learning of High-dimensional Count Data
papers.authors: Linshanshan Wang, Mengyan Li, Zongqi Xia, Molei Liu, Tianxi Cai
papers.abstract: High-dimensional count data arise in many modern applications, such as electronic health records (EHR) and RNA sequencing, with sparse, heterogeneous observations driven by complex latent structure. These characteristics make modeling and prediction challenging, especially when labels are limited. We propose SCORE, a semi-supervised representation learning framework for clustering and embedding construction from high-dimensional count features. SCORE is built on a Poisson-adapted latent factor mixture model that supports incorporating external pre-trained feature embeddings when available, enabling efficient extraction of latent cluster membership and low-dimensional representations. To scale inference and learning to large datasets, SCORE uses a hybrid algorithm that combines expectation-maximization with a Gaussian variational approximation, leveraging a small labeled subset to refine estimation on a large pool of unlabeled samples. We establish convergence guarantees for this hybrid procedure, quantify approximation errors introduced by the Gaussian variational approximation, and derive error rates under increasing embedding dimensions. Our theory and experiments show that incorporating unlabeled data improves accuracy and reduces sensitivity to label scarcity, yielding strong finite-sample performance relative to existing approaches. We demonstrate SCORE for predicting disability status in multiple sclerosis using EHR data, where it learns informative patient embeddings with strong predictive performance, highlighting its practical value.

papers.title: ROC-based methods for comparing two survival curves under non-proportional hazards with right, left, and doubly censored data
papers.authors: Mohammod Mahmudur Rahman, Leonidas E Bantis
papers.abstract: Studies comparing two survival curves to assess treatment differences are commonplace. The widely used log-rank test is designed to operate best under the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. Alternative methods, such as the Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank tests, rely on prior knowledge of survival patterns, which is often difficult to specify before a study. The recently developed MaxCombo test does not require such prior information; however, it leaves substantial room for power improvement, particularly when survival curves cross. To address these issues, we propose new nonparametric and semiparametric methods for comparing two survival curves based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve length and the overlap coefficient, along with a joint inference approach combining both measures. Our methods are applicable under non-PH settings and can accommodate right, left, and double censoring. We evaluate our methods through extensive simulation studies under different non-PH configurations. Our results show improved performance of the proposed methods compared to existing nonparametric methods, particularly under early and crossing effects. Real-world examples involving various non-PH scenarios are provided, illustrating the superiority of our methods in detecting survival differences. We further provide an R package named ''ROCsurvcomp" that implements all our proposed approaches and is available on CRAN.

papers.title: Partially Linear Additive Reversed Mean Model for Panel Count Data With Informative Terminal Event
papers.authors: Anyin Feng, Xiangbin Hu, Wen Su, Xingqiu Zhao
papers.abstract: This article investigates a partially linear additive reversed mean model for panel count data with an informative terminal event. By anchoring the time origin at the terminal event, the proposed model characterizes the recurrent event process prior to the occurrence of the terminal event. The partially linear additive form provides a flexible framework for modeling covariate effects. The B-spline sieve approximation is employed for both the baseline reversed mean function and the link function. To make the optimization of the loss function feasible, we treat the distribution function of the terminal event as a nuisance functional parameter and develop a two-stage estimation procedure. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator, including consistency, convergence rate, and asymptotic distribution. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed estimator performs well in finite-sample settings. The proposed method is further illustrated through an application to the Chinese longitudinal healthy longevity survey (CLHLS).

papers.title: Modeling Amplitude and Phase Variation of Multivariate Random Processes in Metric Spaces*
papers.authors: Yaqing Chen, Kyum Kim
papers.abstract: In functional data analysis, distinguishing between amplitude and phase variation is essential to prevent distorted statistical inferences. While extensive work has been devoted to developing time-warping methods to address this issue for Euclidean functional data, much less is known about how to characterize and model these two sources of variability when they co-exist in random processes taking values in general metric spaces. In this paper, we develop a comprehensive statistical framework characterizing amplitude and phase variation for multivariate metric-space-valued functional data. We propose a geodesic latent deformation model (GLDM) for jointly analyzing both types of variation by using tools from metric geometry, and define tempo indices to quantify the temporal dynamics. We devise a novel estimation procedure and establish (uniform) convergence rates for the model estimators. The method’s broad applicability is demonstrated through a real-world application to annual gender-specific age-at-death distributions providing new insights into global longevity dynamics as well as simulations on multivariate positive semi-definite (PSD) matrix-valued and network-valued functional data.

papers.title: Marginal Analysis of Clustered Interval-Censored Competing Risks Data With Informative Cluster Size
papers.authors: Xinyi Wang, Peijie Wang, Xinyuan Song
papers.abstract: Motivated by the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) study, this paper addresses the marginal analysis of clustered data under a complex setting involving interval censoring, competing risks, and informative cluster size, for which existing methods are not readily applicable. We consider a class of marginal generalized odds-rate transformation models for the cumulative incidence function in the presence of interval-censored competing risks, with the Fine-Gray model and the sub-distribution proportional odds model included as special cases. For statistical inference, a cluster-weighted sieve maximum pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure is developed, in which B-splines are used to approximate the nonparametric components of the semiparametric models. This method effectively reduces the original infinite-dimensional estimation problem to a finite-dimensional one. We establish the asymptotic properties of the resulting parameter estimators and conduct extensive simulation studies to evaluate their finite-sample performance. The proposed methodology is applied to the motivating NACC data to investigate potential risk factors for the cumulative incidence of Lewy body dementia.

papers.title: Joint modeling of longitudinal measurements and survival outcomes in heart valve transplantation data
papers.authors: Avinash Kumar, M S Panwar, Sushil Kumar
papers.abstract: A joint modeling technique for longitudinal data and time-to-event data is advanced statistical methodology to analyze repeated measurements and time-to-event outcomes. In the present article, a shared random effects approach is considered to account for both longitudinal data and survival outcomes. The longitudinal data is submodeled by a linear mixed-effects model that captures the individual response over time. Whereas the time-to-event sub-model uses the generalized exponential distribution as the baseline distribution for the proportional hazard model to incorporate survival times as well as time-independent covariates. To estimate model parameters, the Expectation-Maximization approach has been used, which is effective with latent random effects since random effects are unobservable in nature. In the E-step, the expected log-likelihood is derived based on current parameter estimates, and in the M-step, we maximize this likelihood to update the parameters.
